# Logistic model
```{r, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results=FALSE, output=FALSE}
#Load library so functions run smoothly
library(tidyverse)
#For logit() function
library("gtools")
```

![](images/prevalence.png){style="width:200px; background:white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"}


MaAsLin3 carries out binary logistic regression for prevalence (absence/presence) testing.

## Binary logistics
![](images/binary.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px; border: white solid 5px" fig-align="center"}

Binary logistic regression is used to determine the probability of one of two outcomes.
In MaAsLin3 this is to test prevalence, determining the probability of a feature to be present, given an effect.

With this test we could attempt to answer the following example questions:

- Is _Helicobacter pylori_ more likely to be present in patients with ulcers compared to healthy controls?
- Are _Corynebacterium_ species more likely to be present in the axilla compared to the cheek or scalp?
- Are certain species more likely to be present/detected in samples with higher sampling depth?

We won't go into the workings of binary logistics rather we'll explain its main value: log-odds/logit.

## Log-odds/logit
![](images/coin_toss.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px; border: white solid 5px" fig-align="center"}

Log-odds, also know as the logit, is equal to the logarithm of the odds. The equation is:

$$
logit = ln(p/(1-p))
$$

where:

-   $p$ = Probability
-   $ln$ = natural log

### Surname examples

For example, lets look at the probability of having the surname Murphy if you lived in Ireland in 2014.

-   Probability = 0.0164 (i.e 1.64%)
-   Odds = 0.1752
-   Logit = -4.093938

For a comparison, lets look at the probability of having the surname Gemmell if you lived in Scotland in 2014.

-   Probability = 0.0000446 (i.e 0.00446%)
-   Odds = 0.0000446
-   Logit = -10.01773

In the above case we can see that the logit has a lower negative value for Gemmell which had a lower probability than Murphy. But what is the scale of these values?

### Logit scale

The logit scale goes from negative infinity (probability = 0) to positive infinity (probability = 1). Our anchor point is a probability of 0.5 with a logit value of 0.

Therefore, a positive logit value means the event is more likely than not to occur (\>0.5 probability). Whilst, a negative logit value means the event is more likely to not occur (\<0.5 probability).

Some useful benchmark figures are:

| Probability | Logit       |
|-------------|-------------|
| 1           | Infinite    |
| 0.99        | 4.59512     |
| 0.9         | 2.197225    |
| 0.75        | 1.098612    |
| 0.51        | 0.04000533  |
| 0.5         | 0           |
| 0.49        | -0.04000533 |
| 0.25        | -1.098612   |
| 0.1         | -2.197225   |
| 0.01        | -4.59512    |
| 0           | -Infinite   |

Lets see the equation in the form of a plot:

```{r, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results=FALSE}
base <-
  ggplot() +
    ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(name="Probability", 
                                breaks=seq(from=0, to=1, by=0.1),
                                minor_breaks=seq(from=0.05, to=0.95, by=0.1),
                                limits = c(0,1)) +
    ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(name="Logit", 
                                breaks=seq(from=-10, to=10, by=2),
                                minor_breaks=seq(from=-9, to=9, by=2), 
                                limits = c(-10,10))

base + geom_function(fun = logit, linewidth=1) +
    ggplot2::theme(text=ggplot2::element_text(size = 20))
```

In the plot we can see the logit value slowly changes moving away from a probability of 0.5.
Once the probability is >0.99/<0.01 the logit value quickly increases/decreases getting closer and closer to infinity.
This is the main reason we use logit scale.
It is hard for us to see the difference between a probability of 0.000859 and 0.00006041 but easier for us to differentiate between their logit values of -7.058882 and -9.71429. 

I hope this gives you a clear idea of the log-odds/logit value so you interpret them in future analysis.

More information on how to interpret the logit value is found later in the abundance section: [MaAsLin3 coefficients](/relative/metrics.qmd#coefficients)
